analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC win refunds and disgorgement of profits from companies that defraud consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on May 4, 2022, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and one week later the committee failed to report it favorably, so it never reached the Senate floor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill gives the Federal Trade Commission stronger tools when it sues a company for deceiving consumers. Courts could order the company to refund consumers' money, cancel unfair contracts, and give up profits it made from the wrongdoing, with a 10-year lookback. The FTC had lost much of this ability in a Supreme Court ruling about how the agency could seek monetary redress; this bill was written to restore it. It died in committee a week after introduction.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who were cheated by companies under the FTC's jurisdiction — for example through deceptive advertising, bogus contracts, or scams. They would gain a path to refunds, canceled or corrected contracts, and the return of money or property taken from them [S2] [S3]. The FTC itself benefits: it could ask courts for these remedies rather than being limited to stopping future conduct [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Courts could order restitution for consumer loss, rescission or reformation of contracts, and refund of money or return of property in FTC enforcement suits [S3].
Courts could order disgorgement — surrender of any unjust enrichment a company obtained from the violation, limited to the 10 years before the FTC files suit [S3].

The bill extends the FTC's reach from stopping a practice 'is violating, or is about to violate' to practices a company 'has violated,' allowing money remedies for past conduct, not just injunctions against future conduct [S3].
Time a company spends outside the United States does not count against the 10-year limitations periods, closing an easy way to run out the clock [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that engaged in deceptive practices under FTC jurisdiction would owe refunds, restitution, and up to 10 years of disgorged profits [S3]. Companies in FTC-regulated industries generally would face greater financial exposure in enforcement litigation and stronger incentive to settle, which could translate into modestly higher compliance costs for lawful businesses too.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets courts grant 'any other relief as the court determines to be just and proper' in addition to the listed remedies, which gives judges broad discretion and creates litigation uncertainty for businesses [S3].

A 10-year lookback for restitution and disgorgement reaches far back into a company's past financials, which can be costly and complicated to untangle — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge, though it applies only to companies found to have violated the law [S3].
Restitution and disgorgement amounts are offset against each other, so the combined money judgment against a violator cannot simply stack [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: consumers defrauded under FTC jurisdiction would get a real path to their money back, and the cost falls on companies found liable for deception. The main fair criticism is drafting breadth — the open-ended 'any other relief' clause and the 10-year lookback would give courts wide latitude and create litigation risk beyond the clearest fraud cases. The narrow scope (only FTC-enforced laws, only proceedings begun after enactment) limits spillover [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which failed to report it favorably one week later — a committee vote against moving it forward — and it never received a Senate floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cantwell introduced the bill with Sens. Klobuchar, Warnock, and Lujan on May 4, 2022 [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on May 4, 2022 [S5].
On May 11, 2022, the committee failed to report the bill favorably, effectively ending its advance in the 117th Congress [S5].
The bill accumulated 5 cosponsors — 4 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents — and no Senate Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies under FTC jurisdiction that could have faced refunds and disgorgement of up to 10 years of profits are better off because the bill never advanced, and defrauded consumers got no new remedy.

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

for.name: Sens. Klobuchar, Warnock, and Lujan
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill's introduction as original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Failed to report the bill favorably on May 11, 2022, a week after referral, keeping it from the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote breakdown for the committee action appears in the record; all 5 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, and the sponsor herself chaired this committee in the 117th Congress (well-known public reporting), yet the bill still failed to move forward.

industries.industry: Companies that profit from deceptive practices (direct-to-consumer marketers, telemarketers, firms under FTC jurisdiction)
industries.note: The bill would let courts strip away up to 10 years of profits obtained through deception, order refunds, and cancel unfair contracts [S3]. Their interest in keeping those profits is directly against the consumers the money would go back to.

industries.industry: Lawful businesses regulated by the FTC
industries.note: Companies that follow the rules would not owe restitution or disgorgement, since remedies apply only in enforcement suits over violations [S3], but the broad grant of 'any other relief' and litigation exposure could raise defense and settlement costs across FTC-regulated sectors.
